To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the expression of MHC molecules in the thymic cortex is controlled by the availability of endogenous peptide ligands and that the endogenous MHC class II peptide repertoire tunes the activation thresholds of T cells in the thymocortical microenvironment.

(a) the endogenous peptide ligands presented by MHC class II molecules in the thymic medulla influence the development of T cell receptor ( TCR ) transgenic T cells ; (b) the influence of the endogenous peptide–MHC ligands is exerted by changing the level of expression of molecules that modulate TCR signaling; and (c) this effect is mediated by changes in the expression of the TCR signaling molecule Lck.
self-peptides regulate the development and function of T cells by modulating the expression of T cell activation receptors and signaling molecules.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development and function of T cells, and how they are controlled to ensure tolerance to self-structures.
the mechanisms that control the generation of the T cell repertoire.
understanding the mechanisms that control the activation of T cells, the cells responsible for the immune response against invading microbes and tumor cells.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the endogenous self-peptide–self-MHC ligand repertoire is essential for the development of a T cell repertoire capable of responding to foreign antigens.
T cells are tuned to their self-peptide– MHC ligands in the thymic cortex and that these ligands also modulate the responsiveness of T cells.
the thymic microenvironment is a dynamic one and that the endogenous repertoire of MHC-peptide ligands can modulate T cell reactivity in the thymic environment.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the endogenous self-peptide–self-MHC ligands are not only important in shaping of the T cell repertoire in the thymic selection process but they are also important in setting the T cell reactivity in the periphery

The main takeaway from our work is that
the endogenous repertoire of self-antigencarrying MHC class II molecules is important for setting TCR sensitivity thresholds in the thymic environment.
the self-peptide–Major Histocmpatibility Complex class II (MCH) molecules that are present within the thymus can modulate TCR sensitivity and thereby influence the threshold for T cell activation.
the endogenous self-peptide–class II ligand repertoire shapes the T cell repertoire and tunes the threshold for T cell activation in the thymic cortex.
